extracted.intended_audience: aspiring sketch and improv performers / students of The Groundlings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for writing and performing character-driven sketch and improvised scenes, emphasizing POV, connection, emotional adjustments, and escalation. Focused on workshop/school-level training for stage/TV/film comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-Telling Through Connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers must connect to scene partners and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen to understand (not to respond). Authentic emotion drives connection. Evaluate whether interactions feel genuinely reciprocal and whether performers are attending to each other and the audience, rather than waiting for their turn to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Point of View (clear & consistent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character has a clear POV. POV is consistent across scene. POV is the engine of choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the character's perspective informs choices, language, and objectives throughout the scene and whether the point of view remains coherent rather than shifting opportunistically. A strong POV should generate relationships and conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Adjustment (full, big, real)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters react with full emotional range. Adjustments to new info are big. Real feelings (heightened).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for noticeable, honest emotional shifts when information or circumstances change. Adjustments should be substantial (not slight) and feel true to the character while being heightened for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instant, Enthusiastic Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes-and with energy. No tepid acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether performers embrace offers energetically and build on them. Tepid or half-hearted agreement undermines scene momentum. ‘Yes-and’ should propel the scene forward and open new choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Escalation (heightening/heightened physicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers build scenes through deepening emotional states and physicality. Heighten absurdity AND relatability. Bigger and bigger reactions, never breaking character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the scene escalates via increasing stakes, emotional intensity, and physical commitment while maintaining character truth. Escalation should balance absurdity with relatable beats and avoid actors stepping out of character to signal a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven vs Premise-driven Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it character-driven OR premise-driven (clearly one)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the scene's engine is the character's point of view and choices (character sketch) or a central comedic situation/idea (premise sketch). The piece should clearly commit to one approach rather than muddling both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying Beats
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structure by recognizing the scene's beats—setups, developments, turning points, and payoffs. Clear beats help timing, escalation, and audience comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing for Your Medium
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether choices (pacing, scope, staging, visual gags, dialogue) suit the intended medium. What works onstage may need adaptation for camera or television timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding Material
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the piece originates from strong personal obsessions, distinctive character choices, or high-concept premises. Good source material should sustain escalation and yield specific beats.
